explanations.explanation: Josiah son of Zephaniah, that's the house. Zechariah is told to go there that same day. The text gives us the name and that instruction, and that's all it gives. I'll leave it right there, friend.

Hilkiah son of Shallum shows up in a list of priests' families (1 Chronicles 6:13), but he's not in this passage. The text tells Zechariah to go to the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah. Names come in bunches here, and it's easy to grab the one from another list. I've mixed up a name or two myself, and I had a handle with mine carved in it.

Jesse was David's father (Ruth 4:22), and he's a famous name, so I get why it jumped out. But he's not in this passage. God sends Zechariah to the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah. A big name can steal the spotlight when the quiet one is the right answer.

That's him, friend. The crown goes on the head of the high priest, Joshua son of Jehozadak. God names the head, the metal and the man all in one verse. That's clear directions, and I wish my oven manual was half as clear.

Zerubbabel was the governor of Judah (Haggai 1:1), so a crown on his head sounds like a fair guess. But this verse puts the crown on the head of the high priest, Joshua son of Jehozadak. The text doesn't hand it to anyone else. A governor and a high priest are two different jobs, and this one is the priest's.

Zadok son of Ahitub was a priest in David's day (2 Samuel 8:17), so the priest part of your guess is good. But he's from a different time. The high priest in this passage is Joshua son of Jehozadak, and that's whose head gets the crown. Names in the priest family tree can blur together, so no shame in that.

The temple, yes. The man called the Branch will branch out from His place and build the temple of the LORD. God says it in verse 12 and then says it again in verse 13. When God repeats Himself, friend, you write it down.

A city is a big job, but that's not what the verse says. The Branch will build the temple of the LORD. Verse 13 says it again: "Yes, He will build the temple of the LORD…" It's the same building, said twice.

An altar is a good guess, since it's a holy thing too. But the text says the Branch will build the temple of the LORD. The verse never mentions an altar. Stick close to what's written, friend, and the answer is right there.

A priest, that's right. Verse 13 says, "And He will be a priest on His throne…" So He sits on a throne and rules, and He's a priest right there on it. Two jobs, one throne, and I can barely keep one cookie tray straight.

Prophet is a fair guess, since Zechariah himself is a prophet (Zechariah 1:1) and the whole passage comes through him. But the verse says something else about the Branch. "And He will be a priest on His throne…" He rules, and He is a priest on that throne.

A shepherd is a fair guess, and David is called a shepherd of God's people (2 Samuel 5:2). But this verse doesn't use that word for the Branch. It says the Branch will be a priest on His throne. Stick close to what's written, friend, and the answer is right there.

This one's false, friend. God doesn't say anything about a rivalry. The verse says, "…there will be peaceful counsel between the two." The Branch rules and is a priest on His throne, and the text calls it peaceful.
False is right. The text says, "…there will be peaceful counsel between the two." He rules and He's a priest on His throne, and the word is peaceful. Friend, no rivalry anywhere in that verse.
True. Verse 15 says, "Even those far away will come and build the temple of the LORD…" So the building reaches the ones who are far away. That's a big circle, friend.

It's actually true, so let's fix that. The text says, "Even those far away will come and build the temple of the LORD…" Far-off people are part of this building job. The three exiles in verse 10 came a long way from Babylon, so the idea of people coming from far off is already in the air.

Obey, you got it. The last line says, "This will happen if you diligently obey the voice of the LORD your God." Notice the word diligently. It means this obeying is no half-hearted nod, and I've nodded along at my oven timer plenty of times.

Fear is a good word, and you'll find it all over the Bible. It's just not the word in this verse. The verse says, "…if you diligently obey the voice of the LORD your God." The IF is about obeying His voice.

Remembering matters, and the crown is even called a memorial in verse 14. But the IF at the end uses a different word. It says, "…if you diligently obey the voice of the LORD your God." Remembering is good, friend, and the verse asks for obeying.
